qs.q: Which of the following phases of hemostasis involves von Willebrand factor binding to damaged vessels and platelets to form a temporary plug?
qs.e: During the platelet phase, platelets adhere to the damaged surface with the help of von Willebrand factor to form a temporary plug. The vascular phase instead involves vasoconstriction to reduce blood flow.

qs.q: Which plasma fraction is noted to be the only one that consistently contains von Willebrand factor multimers for the treatment of von Willebrand disease?
qs.e: Cryoprecipitate is a source of fibrinogen, factor VIII, and is the only plasma fraction that consistently contains VWF multimers. DDAVP is another treatment option used to increase plasma VWF.

qs.q: Main function of von Willebrand factor?
qs.e: vWF acts as a bridge between exposed subendothelial collagen and platelet GPIb receptors, initiating primary haemostasis.

ai.title: Von Willebrand Disease
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder caused by quantitative or qualitative defects of von Willebrand factor. It impairs platelet adhesion and reduces factor VIII levels, leading to mucocutaneous bleeding.

sections.p: VWD is a hereditary or acquired deficiency/defect of von Willebrand factor (VWF), a plasma protein that links platelets to subendothelial collagen and stabilises factor VIII.
b: Low VWF antigen or activity confirms the diagnosis
Ristocetin co‑factor activity assesses functional VWF

t.b: Is VWF quantity normal? Low levels indicate quantitative defect (type 1 or 3)
Is VWF functional? Reduced activity points to qualitative defect (type 2)
Does VWF deficiency affect factor VIII? Low FVIII supports VWD, especially type 2N
Does platelet adhesion improve with added VWF? Prolonged closure time supports VWD when other causes excluded
Which VWF multimer pattern is present? Distinguishes type 2 subtypes

sections.p: Severity is graded by VWF antigen/activity levels and clinical bleeding score (e.g., ISTH‑BAT).
b: Mild: >30 % VWF, bleeding only after surgery or trauma
Moderate: 10‑30 % VWF, spontaneous mucosal bleeds
Severe: <10 % VWF, frequent spontaneous bleeds, hemarthroses

sections.p: Most cases are inherited; acquired forms are seen with conditions common in low‑resource settings.
b: Inherited autosomal dominant type 1 (partial quantitative deficiency)
Inherited autosomal recessive type 3 (near‑absent VWF)
Type 2A/2B/2M/2N – qualitative defects
Acquired VWD secondary to: severe liver disease, uremia, hypothyroidism, disseminated malignancy, HIV, malaria, sickle‑cell disease, herbal remedies containing coumarins

sections.p: Bleeding is usually mucocutaneous and proportional to VWF loss.
b: Epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, easy bruising
Prolonged bleeding after circumcision, tooth extraction, or surgery
Rarely, hemarthroses in severe type 3

sections.p: Start with bedside screening, then targeted laboratory tests; adapt when sophisticated assays are unavailable.
b: Bleeding history using a standardized bleeding assessment tool
Basic coagulation screen (PT, aPTT) – aPTT may be prolonged in severe VWD due to low FVIII

t.b: Is factor VIII low enough to affect clotting time? Prolonged aPTT supports severe VWD or factor VIII deficiency
Are platelets normal? Normal count rules out thrombocytopenia as primary cause

t.a: VWF antigen / ristocetin co‑factor (if local lab can run)

t.b: What bedside clues help? Severe mucosal bleeding with normal platelet count and PT, plus prolonged aPTT, points toward VWD

sections.p: Uncontrolled bleeding can be fatal, especially in pregnancy, surgery, or trauma.
b: Intracranial hemorrhage after head injury
Severe postpartum hemorrhage
Life‑threatening gastrointestinal bleed

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, replace VWF, and use adjuncts to support haemostasis.
b: Desmopressin (DDAVP) for type 1 and most type 2A/2M – releases endothelial VWF; avoid in severe cardiac disease or hyponatraemia risk
VWF‑containing concentrate (e.g., Humate‑P) for type 3, type 2B, or DDAVP non‑responders
Tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding when fibrinolysis contributes
Avoid aspirin, NSAIDs and other antiplatelet agents
Treat associated conditions (e.g., antiretroviral therapy for HIV, antimalarials for malaria) that may worsen acquired VWD

sections.p: Regular reassessment of bleeding score and VWF levels guides prophylaxis, especially before surgery or childbirth.
b: Repeat VWF testing after DDAVP trial to document response
Plan prophylactic DDAVP or concentrate before elective procedures
Educate patients on avoiding NSAIDs and reporting new bleeding
Vaccinate against hepatitis B to reduce liver‑related acquired VWD
Platelet function disorders (e.g., Glanzmann thrombasthenia) – normal VWF, abnormal aggregation
Hemophilia A – isolated low factor VIII, normal VWF
Acquired coagulopathy from liver disease – prolonged PT/INR, low multiple factors
Ristocetin co‑factor may be normal in mild type 1 if assay sensitivity low
aPTT can be normal in mild VWD despite low VWF
Pregnancy raises VWF levels, masking deficiency

whenToSeekHelp: Uncontrolled epistaxis or oral bleeding despite local measures
Signs of internal bleeding (abdominal pain, faintness, drop in haemoglobin)
Severe postpartum haemorrhage or bleeding after surgery

faq.q: Why does DDAVP not work in type 2B VWD?
faq.a: DDAVP releases VWF that has increased affinity for platelet GPIb, causing platelet aggregation and thrombocytopenia in type 2B.
Yes, conditions such as severe liver disease, uremia, HIV, malaria, and certain herbal medicines can lower VWF levels or function.

faq.q: What is the role of tranexamic acid in VWD?
faq.a: It inhibits fibrinolysis, helping control mucosal bleeds when VWF replacement is not immediately available.

exam: A 22‑year‑old woman presents with menorrhagia and easy bruising; PT normal, aPTT mildly prolonged. What is the next diagnostic step and why? — Order VWF antigen and ristocetin co‑factor to differentiate VWD from factor VIII deficiency.

During a caesarean section a patient with known VWD type 1 develops sudden oozing despite DDAVP given pre‑operatively. What should you do next? — Give VWF‑containing concentrate because she is a DDAVP non‑responder or has exhausted stored VWF.

A malaria‑endemic region reports increased bleeding after minor trauma. Which acquired cause should be considered and how would you confirm it? — Acquired VWD secondary to malaria; check VWF antigen/activity; if unavailable, treat malaria and observe bleeding response.
Why is desmopressin contraindicated in a patient with severe cardiac disease? — DDAVP can cause fluid retention and hyponatraemia, precipitating heart failure.

A child with severe bleeding has normal platelet count and PT, but aPTT is >45 s. Which disorder is most likely and what confirmatory test is required? — Severe VWD (type 3) or hemophilia A; measure factor VIII activity and VWF antigen to distinguish.

Explain how you would differentiate VWD type 2A from type 2B using laboratory tests. — Multimer analysis shows loss of high‑molecular‑weight multimers in 2A; platelet count falls after ristocetin in 2B, indicating increased platelet binding.

A patient on long‑term NSAIDs develops epistaxis; labs show normal VWF. What is the most likely explanation? — NSAID‑induced platelet dysfunction; VWF studies are normal, so treat by stopping NSAIDs and using topical haemostatic measures.

During pre‑operative assessment you find a low VWF level but the patient reports no bleeding history. How do you proceed? — Repeat testing to confirm; if persistent low VWF, classify as low‑grade VWD and arrange prophylaxis only for high‑risk procedures.
